The Chaotung vole (Eothenomys olitor) is a small murid rodent endemic to montane regions of southwestern China, where it inhabits alpine meadows and shrublands. Basal metabolic rate in this species has been measured at 89.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 89.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under standard respirometry conditions at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a value that appears somewhat elevated relative to predictions based on its adult body mass. Neonates are remarkably small at birth, weighing approximately 2 grams [Wwb = approximately 2 grams], a birth mass that reflects the altricial developmental strategy common among arvicoline rodents. This modest initial size imposes substantial energetic demands on lactating females during the early postnatal period.

Reproductive output in this vole species follows a pattern typical of many small-bodied mammals inhabiting seasonal environments. Field records indicate that females produce litters of 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = 7 pups per litter], and that they can sustain approximately 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters per year] during the breeding season. The gestation period is relatively brief, lasting 24.5 days [tg = 24.5 days] when measured at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration consistent with values reported for other eutherian rodents of comparable body size. Weaning, marking the cessation of maternal provisioning, occurs at 12 days after birth [tx = 12 days after birth] under the same thermal conditions, and the young then transition to a diet of solid vegetation at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C].

Sexual maturation in the Chaotung vole is achieved after a relatively extended juvenile phase compared to some other microtine rodents. Puberty, defined as the attainment of functional reproductive capacity, occurs at 60 days after birth [tp = 60 days after birth] when individuals are maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a delay that likely reflects the time required for sufficient somatic growth and gonadal development. The maximum adult body mass recorded for this species is 34 grams [Wwi = 34 grams], although most field-caught individuals fall within a narrower range of 13 to 15 grams, suggesting that the upper value may be achieved only under exceptionally favorable conditions or by particularly large territorial males. This weight at ultimate size places Eothenomys olitor among the smaller members of its genus.

Longevity data for the Chaotung vole, derived from captive colonies and field recapture studies of the ecologically similar Loxodontomys micropus, indicate that the maximum lifespan is approximately 5.5 years [am = approximately 5.5 years] when measured at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This lifespan is relatively long for a rodent of its size and may be linked to the species' montane habitat, where cooler temperatures and seasonal resource limitations likely slow metabolic aging processes. In comparison with related species such as Eothenomys melanogaster and Eothenomys cachinus, the Chaotung vole exhibits a somewhat slower life-history pace, with delayed reproduction and sustained reproductive output across multiple seasons.

The reproductive physiology of the Chaotung vole is tightly coupled to environmental temperature, as the energetic costs of gestation and lactation are substantial for a mammal of its mass. Experimental studies conducted at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] have confirmed that pregnant females maintain a stable core temperature throughout the 24.5-day gestation period (24.5 days) [tg = 24.5 days], a metabolic challenge that may constrain litter size and weaning success in colder montane microclimates. Field observations further suggest that the narrow birth mass of 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams] represents a critical threshold: neonates below this weight rarely survive to weaning at 12 days [tx = 12 days], whereas slightly heavier pups show markedly improved survival rates at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The interplay between maternal metabolic demands, developmental timing, and neonatal condition likely shapes the species' demographic responses to climate variability in its high-elevation habitat.
